analysis.one_liner: Requires private and state-run prisons holding federal detainees to release records under FOIA.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral; it was introduced with 13 Democratic cosponsors and received no House vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill says that records held by private prisons, jails, and detention facilities that house federal prisoners or detainees must be treated like federal agency records under the Freedom of Information Act, the law that lets the public request government documents. Private prison companies and state or local jails holding people for the federal government would have to disclose the same information federal prisons must disclose, unless a standard legal exemption applies. The federal agencies that pay those facilities would have to write the requirement into their contracts within a year.
analysis.who_benefits: People incarcerated in or detained by private and state/local facilities under federal contracts, their families, journalists, and watchdog groups, who would gain the ability to request records about conditions, medical care, deaths, use of force, and how public money is spent at those facilities. Federal agencies conducting oversight would also get easier access to the records.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Incarcerated people, their families, journalists, watchdogs

how_it_helps.text: Currently, a record held only by a private contractor operating a federal detention facility is generally not subject to FOIA, so the public cannot force its release the way it can with federal Bureau of Prisons records. The bill closes that gap by deeming such records agency records subject to FOIA [S2] [S3].

Facilities could withhold information only where disclosure would cause specific, identifiable harm under an existing FOIA exemption or where disclosure is prohibited by law — the same standard that applies to federal prisons, rather than a looser contractor standard [S3].

The bill makes compliance a material term of federal contracts and requires agencies to modify existing contracts within one year, so the disclosure obligation would attach to current facilities, not just new ones [S3].

Records would have to be kept in searchable, reproducible formats so requests can actually be fulfilled, and the bill explicitly leaves state and local open-records laws intact rather than weakening them [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Private prison and detention contractors, and state or local jails that incarcerate federal detainees under contract, would bear the cost of maintaining, organizing, and releasing records and responding to FOIA requests. The federal agencies that contract with them would bear the cost of writing regulations and administering the new disclosure obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private prison contractors and contracting agencies

drawbacks.text: Contractors and state or local jails would face real administrative costs: maintaining searchable records, processing public records requests, and in some cases building record-keeping systems they do not have today. Those costs would ultimately flow into contract prices paid by taxpayers, at least at the margin [S3].

The bill extends beyond private companies to state and local jails holding federal detainees, so a county jail with a small intergovernmental agreement could be pulled into federal FOIA compliance, raising federalism and burden concerns for local governments [S3].

Supporters of private prisons argue facilities holding federal detainees are already monitored through contract oversight, government audits, and state records laws, so a federal FOIA mandate is a solution in search of a problem and adds compliance costs without clearly improving conditions (a general-knowledge objection; not addressed in the bill text) [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: transparency does not by itself fix prison conditions, but without it, journalists, families, and oversight bodies cannot even see what is happening at facilities where the government has handed custody to a contractor. The main costs are administrative — record-keeping and request-processing — which are modest relative to the size of federal detention contracts, though small county jails holding a handful of federal detainees could feel the burden disproportionately. On balance this is a low-cost, moderate-benefit accountability measure that died before anyone had to weigh it on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jamie Raskin introduced the Private Prison Information Act of 2023 on June 14, 2023, joined by 10 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S1] [S3].
Thirteen members, all Democrats, cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on [S4].

The action history shows only two entries — introduction and referral to Judiciary. No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private prison and detention contractors, and state and local facilities holding federal detainees, are better off because the bill died: they never had to open their records to public FOIA requests. Members of the Judiciary Committee also avoided a vote on a transparency measure that is hard to oppose publicly.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private prison contractors and the committee that stalled it

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans controlling the House and the Judiciary Committee, the bill never moved beyond referral [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Private prison and detention contractors (e.g. companies operating federal detention facilities under contract)
industries.note: The bill would make their records subject to FOIA, exposing conditions, deaths, use of force, and contract spending to public scrutiny for the first time. Their interest in keeping records internal runs directly against the public's interest in seeing how tax-funded detention is run.

industries.industry: State and local jails and correctional systems holding federal detainees under intergovernmental agreements
industries.note: They would face new federal FOIA obligations and record-keeping costs, but the bill does not override or limit state and local open-records laws, and many already face some public-records obligations under their own state laws.

industries.industry: Federal agencies that contract for detention space (e.g. immigration and federal prison authorities)
industries.note: They would bear the cost of writing regulations and modifying contracts, but would gain visibility into contractor operations, which strengthens their own oversight of facilities they pay for.
